messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 77

He is 49, a European man who has spent most of his adult life in fashion, where he is known for his eye for structure and detail. He designs womenswear for a mid-sized label, and before everything changed, his life had a reliable rhythm to it: early mornings in the studio, long afternoons draping fabric on forms, evenings at home with his wife. He still talks about those years as if they belong to another person. The dividing line comes on a winter evening, when his wife is struck by a car while crossing a street a few blocks from their apartment.

He is not with her when it happens. He is at work, pinning a sleeve on a model before a fitting, when his phone keeps vibrating on the cutting table. At first he ignores it, irritated by the interruption. Then he sees an unfamiliar number and answers to a stranger’s voice telling him there has been an accident. He says later that what he remembers most is not panic but a strange precision: the scissors in his hand, the silver pins lined up in a magnetic dish, the model standing motionless while his body seems to turn to ice. He arrives at the hospital and sees his wife unconscious, bruised, surrounded by machinery. For days he lives under fluorescent lights, sleeping upright in waiting room chairs, listening for changes in the tone of monitors. He studies every doctor’s expression as if it is a sketch he must interpret correctly. He cannot shake the thought that he should have been there, should have asked her not to go out, should have picked her up himself.

She survives, but her injuries are severe. The months that follow are filled with surgeries, rehabilitation, and uncertainty. He takes over everything at home while trying to keep working, bringing sketches to the hospital and pretending he can still think creatively in that space. He tells himself he is managing. People admire how devoted he is. Yet from the beginning, something in him remains trapped at the moment of the phone call. He jumps whenever his mobile rings unexpectedly. Sirens on the street below make his chest tighten so abruptly that he has to grip a table to steady himself. Crossing roads becomes a private ordeal. Even when the traffic light changes and other pedestrians move forward, he hesitates at the curb, seeing in a flash not his own body but his wife’s broken one.

At night, the event replays with ruthless inventiveness. He dreams of arriving too late, of hospital corridors that lengthen as he runs, of his wife calling out to him from the opposite side of a road he cannot cross. Sometimes he wakes disoriented and reaches across the bed to make sure she is breathing. On the nights she sleeps deeply, he lies awake listening for movement. If she shifts or murmurs, he bolts upright. In the morning he is exhausted, but he cannot rest during the day either. His mind circles the same questions—what if she had left five minutes later, what if he had called her, what if this means the world can collapse at any second and without warning.

His work begins to suffer in ways that embarrass him. Fashion had once been the place where he felt most fluid and alive. Now his concentration fractures. In fittings he loses track of what has just been said. A junior assistant asks a simple question about seam placement, and he stares blankly before realizing he has not heard a word. He avoids designing certain silhouettes because the reflective materials and metallic trims remind him of emergency vehicles and surgical equipment. During one collection meeting, a colleague suggests staging the runway show around the theme of “impact,” and he feels a wave of nausea so sudden he has to leave the room and lock himself in a toilet stall until the shaking passes. He tells others he has migraines.

Outside work, his world narrows. He no longer meets friends for dinner because restaurants require crossing busy intersections and enduring the chaos of city noise. He takes long detours on foot to avoid the street where his wife was hit. If she is delayed getting home, he calls repeatedly, then hates the edge in his own voice when she answers. He knows his vigilance feels suffocating to her, and this fills him with shame, but he cannot seem to stop. He startles when she drops a pan in the kitchen. He scans her face constantly for signs of pain or fatigue, as if disaster might announce itself in miniature before striking again.

He is aware that the accident happened to her, not to him, and this thought becomes another source of torment. He dismisses his own suffering as indulgent, then feels blindsided by it anyway. He cries unexpectedly while steaming a garment, while waiting at a traffic light, while folding his wife’s coat over the back of a chair. He has become, in his own words, “a man who is always braced.” Even now, years after the accident, with his wife back at home and outwardly recovered more than anyone first hoped, he lives as though catastrophe remains only seconds away.
